title: The Castle That Made Kings
subtitle: Warwick Castle → Lord Leycester → the Beauchamp Chapel
intro: One castle, one town, 958 years — from a pile of mud in 1068 to a gold tomb finished in 1464. Five acts, three live shows, three things to say at every stop. Leave at 9:30, camera down by 4:45.

dayGlance.title: Origins & the Fortress
dayGlance.sub: 10:30 AM — the Norman mound, then the great towers.

dayGlance.title: The Kingmaker & the House
dayGlance.sub: 11:45 AM — jousting, falconry, the trebuchet at 2, then the State Rooms.

dayGlance.title: Dudley & the Tombs
dayGlance.sub: 3:25 PM — Lord Leycester, the Beauchamp Chapel, then the river. Done by 4:45.

acts.label: Act 1 · The Norman beginning
acts.tagline: 1068. An earth mound and a decision.
acts.narrative: Set the day up outside at Castle Bridge, then go in and climb the Mound first — because that mound IS the original castle. In 1066 William of Normandy invaded from France, killed the English king and took the crown. Two years later he ordered this built. A few thousand Normans were holding down two million English, and castles were how they did it.

acts.label: Act 2 · The fortress
acts.tagline: Three hundred years later, the Beauchamps build in stone.
acts.narrative:
The trebuchet at 10:45 explains medieval war better than any caption: a few rocks an hour never knocked a castle down, so sieges were months of starvation with a machine making noise.

Then the towers, and the good bit — who paid. Thomas Beauchamp built both between 1330 and 1360 with ransom money from French noblemen he captured at Crécy and Poitiers. Caesar's Tower is also called Poitiers Tower: the prisoners were held in the basement and their ransoms built the walls around them.

acts.label: Act 3 · The Kingmaker
acts.tagline: One earl, two kings deposed, dead at 42.
acts.narrative:
Explain the Wars of the Roses before you explain the Kingmaker, or the Kingmaker means nothing. Thirty years of civil war, 1455 to 1485, two branches of one royal family, red rose against white.

Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, was the richest man in England. He put Edward the Fourth on the throne in 1461, fell out with him, then switched sides and restored Henry the Sixth in 1470. England had no standing army — kings borrowed soldiers from nobles — so the richest noble picked the king. He died at Barnet in 1471 and took four centuries of family power with him.

acts.label: Act 4 · The long afterlife
acts.narrative:
A castle stays a castle only while somebody needs to defend it. Gunpowder made tall walls pointless and England stopped fighting itself, so the Greville family spent 374 years turning a fortress into a house — and sold it to a waxwork company in 1978.

Then the Mill and Engine House: the only part of the site built to do a job, where Victorian engineers wired a medieval castle for electric light before the town had any.

acts.label: Act 5 · The tombs
acts.tagline: You walked their rooms. Now stand at their graves.
acts.narrative:
Walk into town at 2:40 and introduce Robert Dudley at the Lord Leycester, because you'll be at his grave within the hour. Dudley is the man Elizabeth the First probably loved and never married. In 1571 he turned medieval guild buildings here into a home for wounded soldiers — and it still is one.

Then the ending. The gilded tomb in the Beauchamp Chapel holds Richard Beauchamp, the English commander at Rouen who oversaw Joan of Arc's trial and execution in 1431. Dudley is buried in the same room. You spend a day in the rooms these men built, and finish standing over both of them.

kit: Phone or camera, plus a spare battery — you're recording on and off for six and a half hours
A clip mic or AirPods if you have them — the show arenas are open and windy
Shoes you can climb two towers in
A light layer — 12°C at 9 AM, 20°C by mid-afternoon
Contactless for parking (£10), Lord Leycester (£9) and the chapel (£5)
preTrip: Book the Warwick Castle standard day ticket online tonight — and do NOT add the Dungeon
Do NOT pre-book Lord Leycester — the 25% castle discount only works at their door
Charge every battery, clear the card
Set phone alarms for 10:40, 11:40 and 12:25 — the three shows are the spine of the day
At the gate, check the show board and confirm 10:45 / 11:45 / 12:30 haven't moved
goldenRule: The three shows are fixed points — 10:45, 11:45, 12:30. Everything else bends around them. Miss one and you lose an act.

days.planHeader: One castle, five acts · 9:30 AM – 4:45 PM

planNote.text: Out of Mariner Avenue at 9:30, about 45 minutes, park at the Stables car park (CV34 4QU, £10) around 10:15. Two changes because of the later start: the trebuchet is now the 2 PM show instead of 10:45, and the river shot moves to the end of the day at 4:35 — which is better light anyway. Fixed times you must hit: jousting 11:45, falconry 12:30, trebuchet 2:00. Met Office for Warwick: sunny intervals 8 AM to 6 PM, 12 up to 20°C, under 5% rain. Lord Leycester's last admission is 4 PM and St Mary's shuts at 5 — the plan gets you into both with room to spare.

planArrival.title: Camera down at 4:45 PM
planArrival.note: Five minutes back to the Stables car park, about 45 minutes home. In by roughly 5:35 — seven hours door to door.

castle-bridge.name: Castle Bridge & the River Avon
castle-bridge.story: This is the shot the video opens with, and you're filming it at the end of the day. That's normal — shooting order and edit order are different things. It's also better light: the low afternoon sun comes round onto the river front, which you'd never get at half nine in the morning. Stand here, say the opening lines, and you're done.
facts: There's been a castle on this rock for 958 years, since 1068. Almost every other English castle is a ruin today — this one survived because people never stopped living in it. A family was still here until 1978.

That big tower has been nicknamed Caesar's Tower for centuries, but Caesar never came near England's midlands. Someone invented the name later because it sounded grand. Its real name is Poitiers Tower, after a battle in France in 1356 — and I'll show you why that matters.

Those broken stone arches sticking out of the river are the old medieval bridge. When it wore out in 1793 nobody demolished it. They built a new bridge next door and left the old one standing in the water.

routeCard.sub: Castle Bridge, Banbury Road · 4:35 PM · free
routeCard.note: Five minutes' walk from the Stables car park, so it costs you almost nothing on the way out.

see: The castle's south front in morning light
planCard.todo: Last stop, on the walk back to the car. Film your opening here — the hook, what the day is, and the promise about Joan of Arc's tomb. Then finish.

the-mound.name: The Mound
the-mound.story: This lump of earth IS the original castle. Everything else on this site was built later, on top of it. If you get this bit across, the rest of the day makes sense.
facts: In 1066 William, Duke of Normandy — that's northern France — sailed across the Channel, killed the English king in battle and took the crown by force. Two years later, in 1068, he ordered this mound built. He was a foreign king ruling a country that hated him.

And there were only a few thousand Normans holding down around two million English. Castles were how they managed it — you can't rebel against a fortress you can't get inside. William built a chain of them across the country, and this is one.

A castle like this went up in weeks, not years: make the locals pile up earth, stick a wooden tower on top, done. Every stone building you can see around you came 300 years later. This mound of dirt is the only piece of the original 1068 castle left standing.

routeCard.sub: Inside the castle grounds · gates open 10:00
routeCard.note: All the castle stops are one walk, not separate drives.

see: Views over the whole castle site
The grounds Capability Brown landscaped from 1749
planCard.todo: First thing in. One idea only: 1068, a foreign king, and a country he had to hold down. Don't rush this one — it sets up everything else.

trebuchet.name: The Legend of the Trebuchet
trebuchet.angle: Why sieges took months, not days
trebuchet.story: The show is called The Legend of the Trebuchet and there's no legend attached to this particular machine — it's a modern rebuild from medieval drawings. But there IS a famous trebuchet story, and it's worth telling while you wait for them to load it.
facts: A trebuchet is basically a giant see-saw. You winch a huge weight up on the short end, drop it, and the long arm whips round and slings a rock. This one is 18 metres tall and weighs 22 tonnes — the biggest working one in the world.

Here's the story worth telling. In 1304 King Edward I built the largest trebuchet ever made to attack Stirling Castle in Scotland and nicknamed it Warwolf. It took about 50 men three months to build and 30 wagons to move. The 30 defenders inside tried to surrender before it was even finished — and Edward refused to let them, because he wanted to see it work first.

Watch how long the crew take to load one single shot. That's the whole point: a few rocks an hour never knocked a castle down. The machine was there to terrify people and wear them out. What actually beat a castle was starvation, and that takes months.

routeCard.sub: River bank, below the castle · 2:00 PM show
routeCard.note: Included in your day ticket. Get there 5 minutes early for a clear sightline.

planCard.todo: The 2 PM show. Be there by 1:50. Tell the Warwolf story while they winch it up — that's the dead time. In the edit this belongs back with the towers, before the jousting.

towers.name: Guy's Tower, Caesar's Tower & the Ramparts
towers.angle: French prisoners paid for these walls
towers.story: This is where the castle stops being mud and wood and becomes the fortress you see from the road. The interesting part is who paid for it. Thomas Beauchamp, Earl of Warwick, built both towers between 1330 and 1360, and he funded it with the profits of war in France — he commanded at the Battle of Crécy in 1346 and fought at Poitiers in 1356. He rebuilt the town church with ransom money too, from a French archbishop he captured.
facts: Both towers went up between 1330 and 1360, built by Thomas Beauchamp, Earl of Warwick — 300 years after that mound of earth, once his family had become seriously rich.

And here's how medieval war actually worked: if you captured a French nobleman you didn't kill him, you held him until his family paid to get him back. That ransom money built these towers. Caesar's Tower's other name is Poitiers Tower, because prisoners from that battle were kept in the basement — their ransoms paid for the walls they were locked inside.

Look at Guy's Tower: twelve sides, not four. Attackers used to dig away a square tower's corner until the whole thing collapsed. Take the corners away and there's nothing to dig at. The shape itself is the defence.

routeCard.note: Steep, narrow spiral stairs and no lift. Take it slowly.

walkPoints.name: Guy's Tower
walkPoints.story: Twelve-sided, about 39 metres, five storeys of guest chambers stacked above each other. Built to impress as much as defend.
walkPoints.todo: Climb this one first while your legs are fresh.

walkPoints.name: The ramparts
walkPoints.story: The curtain wall walk linking the two great towers, looking down into the courtyard on one side and out over the Avon on the other.
walkPoints.todo: Walk it slowly — best views over the river and down into the courtyard.

walkPoints.name: Caesar's Tower
walkPoints.story: The taller of the two at roughly 44 metres, with a dungeon in the basement that held French knights captured at Poitiers in 1356.
walkPoints.todo: Mention the dungeon and the French prisoners. It lands better than the height does.

see: Views over the Avon and the courtyard
planCard.todo: Both towers and the wall between them in 30 minutes. Steep narrow stairs — take it slowly. Be seated for the jousting at 11:45.

jousting.name: Wars of the Roses LIVE
jousting.angle: The man who chose the King of England — twice
jousting.story: Centre of the whole story, so set it up properly before the show starts. People need to know what the Wars of the Roses even were before the Kingmaker means anything.
facts: First, what the Wars of the Roses actually were: a civil war that ran on and off for 30 years, 1455 to 1485, between two branches of the same royal family. The Lancastrians used a red rose as their badge, the Yorkists a white one. Cousins killing cousins over the crown.

Now the man from this castle. Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, was the richest nobleman in England. In 1461 he put Edward the Fourth on the throne. Then Edward crossed him — so in 1470 Warwick changed sides and put the old king, Henry the Sixth, back. He made two kings and broke two. People started calling him the Kingmaker.

How can one earl do that? Because England had no standing army. When a king went to war he had to ask his nobles to bring their men — and Warwick had more land, more money and more soldiers than anybody. Whoever he backed, won. He was killed at the Battle of Barnet in 1471, and 400 years of Warwick power died with him.

routeCard.note: Included in the day ticket. Seats fill — get there by 11:40.

see: The castle's south front as backdrop
planCard.todo: Tell all three of these before it starts, while the arena fills up. Then just watch.

falconry.name: The Falconer's Quest
falconry.angle: The most expensive hobby in medieval Europe
falconry.story: Not strictly part of the castle's story, but hunting with birds is what earls actually did with their afternoons for 500 years. The language angle is the one people remember.
facts: Falconry was ranked by law. A 15th-century English handbook lists exactly which bird you were allowed to fly according to your rank — an eagle for an emperor, a peregrine for an earl, a kestrel for a servant. The bird on your arm announced your status before you said a word.
A trained hawk could cost more than a horse, and taming one took months of daily work. It was the most expensive hobby in medieval Europe, which is precisely why nobles did it.

Three phrases you use all the time come from this. 'Hoodwinked' — falcons wear a little leather hood over the eyes to keep them calm, so to hoodwink someone was literally to blindfold them. 'Bated breath' — a tethered hawk that panics and beats its wings is bating, so waiting with bated breath is holding yourself still out of nerves. And 'haggard' — a haggard was a wild adult hawk you could never fully tame, which is why it now means someone who looks worn out.

routeCard.note: Included in the day ticket. Sit on the grassed slope for the cleanest sky behind the birds.

see: Eagles, vultures and owls in flight
planCard.todo: Last outdoor stop. After this the weather stops mattering.

lunch.name: Lunch — thirty minutes
lunch.angle: Halfway, and the hard part is already filmed
lunch.story: Halfway. All three shows are done and the outdoor half of the day is behind you. Everything from here is indoors.

routeCard.sub: Inside the castle grounds · 30 minutes, no longer

see: Somewhere to sit down for half an hour
planCard.todo: Sit down properly for 35 minutes. The trebuchet is at 2, so you've got time.

state-rooms.name: Great Hall & State Rooms
state-rooms.angle: When a fortress stops needing to be one
state-rooms.story: A castle only stays a castle while somebody needs to defend it. This is the room where that stops being true and the whole place turns into a rich family's house.
facts: The Greville family owned this castle for 374 years, from 1604 to 1978. By their time nobody needed to defend it — gunpowder had made tall stone walls pointless, and England had stopped fighting itself. So they turned a fortress into a very grand home.
A fire in 1871 burned out part of this range. What they put back was built to look old, so a good deal of what you're walking through is Victorian work pretending to be medieval.
In 1978 the family ran out of money and sold the entire castle to Madame Tussauds, the waxwork museum company. That is how a Norman fortress ended up as a tourist attraction with a jousting show.

routeCard.note: Low light indoors — handheld, brace against door frames rather than pushing the ISO.

planCard.todo: Say the turn out loud: this is where the castle stops being a weapon and becomes a house.

mill-engine.name: Mill & Engine House
mill-engine.angle: The only part built to do a job
mill-engine.story: Down by the river under the big tower. Least visited corner of the site and genuinely one of the most interesting.
facts: This is the only part of the castle built to do actual work rather than for war or for showing off. There's been a mill on this spot since the Middle Ages, using the river to grind grain.
In the 1890s the family installed generators in here and wired the castle for electric light — years before most of the town of Warwick had any. If you were rich enough, you got electricity first.
Same building, same river, 700 years apart: water power, then electric power. Nobody knocked it down, they just kept finding new uses for it.

routeCard.note: Steps down and back up. Last castle stop — leave by 2:40 for the walk into town.

see: The medieval bridge arches from the far bank
planCard.todo: Quick stop. The broken bridge arches from this morning are right outside, seen from the other bank.

lord-leycester.name: The Lord Leycester
lord-leycester.angle: The man who nearly married the Queen
lord-leycester.story: Ten minutes' walk from the castle gate. You have to introduce Robert Dudley properly here, because in half an hour you'll be standing at his grave and the name needs to mean something by then.
facts: Start with who he was. Robert Dudley is the man Queen Elizabeth the First probably loved. She ruled England from 1558 to 1603 and never married anybody — and for years the whole country assumed she would marry Dudley. She never did. He stayed close to her his entire life and never quite got there.

In 1571 Dudley took a set of 200-year-old guild buildings here and turned them into a home for wounded soldiers. Careful with the word: back then a 'hospital' didn't mean medicine, it meant a charitable house that took people in. And it still does the job — retired servicemen live here today, 455 years later.

Look at this timber, then look at the brick buildings on either side. In 1694 a fire burned down most of the centre of Warwick and this survived it. That's why it's the odd one out — everything around it had to be rebuilt afterwards.

routeCard.sub: High Street · open till 5, last admission 4
routeCard.note: Buy at the door, NOT online — the 25% castle discount only works at their ticket office.

planCard.todo: Show your Warwick Castle ticket at the desk for 25% off — £9 instead of £12.

beauchamp-chapel.name: St Mary's — The Beauchamp Chapel
beauchamp-chapel.angle: The ending — the man who burned Joan of Arc
beauchamp-chapel.story: This is the payoff for the whole day, and it's a big one. The man in the gold tomb ran Joan of Arc's trial. Tell that, then link back to the castle you started at this morning, and stop.
facts: The man in the gilded tomb is Richard Beauchamp, Earl of Warwick, from the same family that built those towers. In 1431 he was the English commander in charge of Rouen in France — and Rouen is where Joan of Arc was held prisoner. He oversaw her trial and he was there when they burned her. He even sent his own doctor to keep her alive long enough to be tried.

He died in France in 1439 and his body was brought home. This chapel was then built specially to hold him: 21 years of work, from 1443 to 1464, at enormous cost. His effigy is gilt bronze, and notice the hands — raised, but not pressed together. That's deliberate. He's meant to be looking at a vision, not praying.

And Robert Dudley is buried in this same room — the man whose soldiers' home you walked out of half an hour ago. His little son is here too, dead at three years old. Two men, four centuries of this one town, in a room you can cross in five steps.

routeCard.note: Open from 10:30 on Saturdays and closes at 5, so 3:30 is comfortable. Chapel and chancel are £5 on the door.

planCard.todo: Pay the £5 for the chapel — this is the ending. Say your closing line here. Then one short walk to the river for the opening shot and you're finished.

coldOpen.title: Cold open
coldOpen.where: Castle Bridge, before you go in — 9:20 AM
facts: The hook: 'this castle chose the King of England — twice'
What this is: one castle, one town, one day. From a pile of mud in 1068 to a solid gold tomb finished in 1464.
The promise: 'and it ends ten minutes' walk from here, at the tomb of the man who sent Joan of Arc to the stake'

signOff.title: Closing sign-off
facts: Where you are: standing over the man who ran Joan of Arc's trial — and he's from the castle you started at this morning
The shape of the day: a mud mound at ten this morning, a gold tomb at four this afternoon. Four hundred years, one town, one walk.
The ask: like, subscribe — and where should the next one go?

talkTipbox: Assume your viewer knows none of this. Every time you say a name — Dudley, Beauchamp, the Kingmaker — give them one line on who that is before you go on, or it means nothing. Three facts a stop, and you only need to land the one that grabbed you. Date, what happened, why it's surprising. Then move.
goldenRules: Three fixed show times: jousting 11:45, falconry 12:30, trebuchet 2:00. Everything bends around them.
Confirm those on the board at the gate — they do move.
Keep your castle ticket on you: it's 25% off at Lord Leycester (£9 not £12).
£5 for the Beauchamp Chapel — that's the ending, don't skip it.
Be at Lord Leycester by 3:55 at the latest. Last admission is 4 PM, no exceptions.
Talk before each show starts, not over the top of it.
The river shot is last, at 4:35 — but it's the opening of the video.
outro: One castle, 958 years, and you finish standing at their tombs. That's a film, not a tour.
